subject: mathematics
question_text: Prove that sin(π/5) sin(2π/5) sin(3π/5) sin(4π/5) = 5/16.

mark_split.label: Substitute the exact values and square

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 8 TRIGONOMETRIC RATIOS, Very Short Answer question 36(i), book p.91. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The two marks sit on the product-to-sum step and on the closing substitution; folding the two supplementary angles stays on the page as unmarked working. Paper position: Maths-1A Section A runs Q1-Q10 at 2 marks each, all compulsory, and Trigonometric Ratios and Transformations holds two of those ten slots. NUMERIC CHECK before authoring: the product was evaluated to 12 decimal places as 0.312500000000, which is exactly 5/16. recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this one — name each move in order.

page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: Fold the supplementary angles
steps.margin_note: π/5 = 36° and 2π/5 = 72°. The last two angles are 180° minus the first two, so the whole product is [sin 36° sin 72°] squared.

recall.must_convey: That sin(3π/5) = sin(2π/5) and sin(4π/5) = sin(π/5), so the product is [sin 36° sin 72°]².
accept: sin of pi minus theta is sin theta so the last two repeat the first two
three pi by five is the supplement of two pi by five
the product becomes sin thirty six sin seventy two whole squared
supplement kabatti last rendu first rendu laage untayi
fold the last two angles onto the first two

steps.why: The third and fourth angles are the supplements of the second and first, so the four-factor product is the square of a two-factor product.
common_mistakes: Writing sin(π − θ) as −sin θ, which is the rule for cosine.
Leaving all four factors and trying to work out each one.
steps.memory_tip: sin(π − θ) = sin θ, so the last two factors repeat the first two.

steps.label: Apply 2 sin A sin B
steps.margin_note: First mark. cos(36° − 72°) = cos(−36°) = cos 36°, and cos 108° is negative because 108° is in the second quadrant.
lines: 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B)

recall.must_convey: That 2 sin A sin B = cos(A − B) − cos(A + B) gives cos 36° + cos 72° after reducing cos 108°.
accept: two sin a sin b is cos of a minus b minus cos of a plus b
cos one o eight is minus cos seventy two
so twice the product is cos thirty six plus cos seventy two
product ni cosines sum ga marchali
use the product to sum formula for two sines
reject: the answer is five by sixteen

steps.why: Turning the product into a sum of cosines is what brings in 36° and 72°, the two angles of this chapter whose exact cosines are known.
common_mistakes: Using cos(A + B) − cos(A − B), which gives the wrong sign.
steps.memory_tip: In 2 sin A sin B the difference comes first and the sum second, with a minus between.

steps.label: Substitute the exact values and square
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The sum of the two cosines is √5/2, so the single product is √5/4, and the answer is that squared.

recall.must_convey: That cos 36° + cos 72° = √5/2, so sin 36° sin 72° = √5/4 and the product is 5/16.
accept: the two cosines add to root five by two so the product is root five by four
square root five by four to get five by sixteen
the one cancels and the root five doubles
root five by four square chesthe five by sixteen
the answer is five by sixteen
reject: use the product to sum formula for two sines

steps.why: Adding the two exact cosines cancels the 1 and doubles the √5. Squaring at the end is what turns √5 into 5 and 4 into 16.
common_mistakes: Forgetting to divide by 2 before squaring.
Squaring only the numerator and leaving the denominator as 4.
steps.memory_tip: √5/4 squared is 5/16: the root disappears and the 4 becomes 16.
